Histoire des Aït Bouguemez — une page documentaire complète sur la vallée des Aït Bouguemez dans le Haut Atlas central, de la préhistoire à octobre 2026, avec une distinction explicite, en chaque endroit, entre ce qui est documenté, ce qui est hypothèse et ce qui est récit oral.

Contenu préparé à partir de sources publiées lues le 30 octobre 2026 ; les chiffres et les faits sont attribués à leurs sources dans le corps de la page et dans la section Sources.

Central High Atlas · Azilal Province · Béni Mellal – Khénifra Region

History of Aït Bouguemez

“The Happy Valley” — from dinosaur tracks to apple orchards

This valley's history is not the history of a state or a city. It is the history of a mountain society that was both farming and herding at once, kept its de facto independence for centuries, organised its water and pastures through precise custom, and guarded its harvests in collective granaries — until the paved road, apples and tourism transformed its face in just two decades.

Site prepared byBadr Allali

1,800 – 2,000 mAltitude of the valley floor, stretching about 25 km
4,068 mIghil M'Goun peak, overlooking the valley from the south
12th centuryFirst known written mention, by the historian al-Baydhaq
16,401 peoplePopulation of Tabant commune in the 2024 census

Cover photo: the valley floor and its green fields beneath the M'Goun peaks. Photos used on this page are credited to their sources in the Sources section.

GeographyPrehistoryName & tribesTranshumance & waterDynasties & zawiyasLand of sibaProtectorate & resistanceAfter independenceSociety & architectureHeritageTimelineDocumented & oralSourcesContact
How to read this page: every important claim is tagged with its level of confidence: DocumentedA written, academic or official source Research hypothesisProposed by researchers, not settled Oral accountCirculated by residents, not documentarily verified

Most of what concerns Aït Bouguemez itself falls into the second and third categories, not the first. The reason is structural: an isolated mountain valley, far from the cities where news was written down, with — apparently — no old local written archive. Anyone seeking its history must read it through the history of its wider neighbourhood: Haskoura, Demnate, the Zawiya of Ahansal, the Aït Atta, and the whole central High Atlas.

Chapter One

Geography: why history was made here in this shape

Geographic enclosure is the key to the whole history: narrow passes that are easy to watch, snowy winters that isolate the valley for months, fertile soil and permanent water — a society able to be self-sufficient, and hard to subdue from outside.

Borders of the valley

The valley lies on the northern slope of the central High Atlas. It is bounded to the north by Ighil n'Tizal (3,034 m), to the east by the Adrar Azourki massif (3,682 m) and Lake Izoughar, to the south by Ighil Waougoulzat (3,593 m) and then the Ighil M'Goun massif (4,068 m), and it opens westwards onto the Aït Bou Oulli valley beneath Mount Rat.

Its floor is relatively flat and cultivated, sloping from 2,000 m in the east to 1,800 m in the west, with its administrative centre Tabant in the middle — also the name of the rural commune that today matches most of the valley.

A valley shaped like a Y

The Assif n'Aït Hakim and Assif n'Touaya streams meet near Tabant, at the foot of the Ighrem of Sidi Moussa, to form the Assif Bouguemez, which flows into the Lakhdar river together with the Assif Bou Oulli.

People today live in about 27–32 douars (villages) — the number varies by census year and by the definition of a douar; no single statistical source settles it.

Source: valley description and borders in French Wikipedia, “Vallée des Aït Bouguemez”.

Chapter Two

Prehistory: dinosaurs, an ancient lake, and engravings with no firm date

Dinosaur tracks at Ibakallioune Geologically documented

The valley's oldest “history” is not human at all. At the douar of Ibakallioune, on limestone slabs from the Middle Lias (Lower Jurassic, about 183–185 million years ago), clear dinosaur footprints can be seen: huge herbivorous sauropods and carnivorous theropods. The site has become one of the most famous in the M'Goun Geopark.

Do not confuse the two: these tracks do not indicate human settlement. They show that hundreds of millions of years ago the area was a shallow coastal plain crossed by giant reptiles.

The lake that made the plain Geomorphologically documented

An ancient rockfall at Tizi n'Tighza, at the valley's lower western end, formed a natural dam in the Lower Pleistocene. An ancient lake then covered the whole valley and deposited the silt that formed its present flat floor, before the river cut through the dam and carved the Jrou gorge. The valley's fertile “plain” itself is therefore a geological product, not just ordinary farmland.

Rock engravings at Tizi n'Tirghist Hypothesis — dating not settled

The closest archaeological evidence of ancient human presence near the valley is important rock engravings in neighbouring Aït Bou Oulli, at the foot of Mount Rat, at about 2,500 m, near the passes linking the Sahara to the interior. Two researchers offered different readings of the drawings:

  • Clor: Berber invaders commemorating a battle they fought over pastures and won; drawings of camel and ostrich suggest the battle was on the plain.
  • Simonneau: warrior herders who took refuge in the mountains as the Sahara dried between 2500 and 1200 BCE.

Researcher Mohamed Khouya himself warns against trusting either reading, especially the dating, though he considers it almost certain that an important battle took place nearby and a victory was commemorated. Recent press estimates put some engravings at about 4,500 years old — a journalistic estimate, not laboratory dating.

Khouya also notes remains of primitive dwellings in caves along the riverbanks, which residents attribute to “the Portuguese”. Oral account This attribution does not mean an actual Portuguese presence — the Portuguese never penetrated the central Atlas — but is likely folk memory attaching every unknown ancient trace to a foreign “other”. The question still awaits archaeological excavation that has not yet been done.

Methodological warning: there are no excavations or texts that allow dating the first permanent settlement of the valley floor itself. The formula common in tourist writing — “Berbers have lived here unchanged since 3000 BCE” — is a general statement about North Africa, with no specific evidence for Aït Bouguemez, and it implies a false immobility: the society changed a great deal in its composition, language and economy. The valley was a passage before it was a home, and the passage gradually became a home as herders who combined herding and farming settled.
Chapter Three

The name and the tribes: “people of the middle” and a human mosaic

Aït Bouguemez = people of the middle Linguistic interpretation

“Aït” means “people of / sons of”, and “Bouguemez” is explained in the most widely circulated interpretation as “people of the middle” or “people of the centre” (from “ammas” = middle), because the valley lies at the heart of the central High Atlas. Some pages also give the form “Aït Bou Ammas” as the origin of the name, with the same meaning.

The meaning matches a linguistic fact: the valley sits on the boundary between Tachelhit (to the south and west) and Central Atlas Tamazight (to the north and east) — it really is a linguistic and geographic “middle”. Its people today mainly speak Central Atlas Tamazight, with a presence of Darija and some French.

The name is spelled variously: Aït Bouguemez, Aït Bougoumez, and in Arabic script in several forms. Do not confuse “Aït Bouguemez” (the tribe and valley) with “Tabant” (the administrative centre and commune).

Why “the Happy Valley”? Widely circulated account

The nickname “the Happy Valley” (Vallée heureuse) is relatively recent: the circulated explanation is that it was coined by foreign visitors taken by the residents' hospitality and joy at summer and autumn celebrations (weddings, festivals, harvests), and by the valley's fertility and mild climate — some German sources even mention the possibility of two harvests a year depending on snow and rain.

There is no evidence the nickname is old or official, and it has not been attributed to a specific traveller or book; today it is the valley's best-known marketing name.

Source: explanation of the nickname at SNRT; dialect boundary in French Wikipedia.

First written mention: al-Baydhaq and the Sanhaja of the Shade Textually documented — a single reference

Khouya confirms that the first reference to reach us is in al-Baydhaq (historian of the Almohad movement, 12th century), in his book “Al-Ansab fi Ma'rifat al-Ashab”, where he classified the Aït Bouguemez among the Sanhaja of the Shade, which he divided into Bani Aït Kafou and Bani Sattat — the Aït Bouguemez, together with the Jrawa, belonging to the fifth section of Bani Sattat. The reference does not allow their territory to be pinpointed, beyond that they were on the northern slopes of the central High Atlas.

The name then disappeared from texts for centuries, returning only in very late sources: “Ad-Durra al-Jalila” by Abdullah al-Khalifti, writings of travellers such as Charles de Foucauld, then ethnographers such as Émile Laoust. Khouya attributes this silence to the encirclement of the Haskoura of the Shade by the Arab Banu Hilal from the north (from the 13th century) and the Banu Ma'qil from the Drâa side, to Demnate's role as “capital of the Haskouris” hiding what lay behind it, and to the valley's difficult terrain. Plausible explanations — but they remain explanations, not texts.

The three fractions

Aït Hakim

East of the valley, on the Assif n'Aït Hakim — one of the valley's two branches that meet at Tabant.

Aït Mahia

Also spelled Aït Mihia. Inside each fraction are “bones” (ighsan): large patrilineal families descended from one ancestor, and inside each “bone”, families (takat).

Aït Ouriaat

Also spelled Aït Wriaat. Locations moved between fractions through alliances — such as Aït Imi, which was Aït Mahia and then became Aït Ouriaat.

Newcomers and a mosaic, not one lineage

Alongside the old core came later elements: the Iklawan group, apparently from southern Glaoua (one of the components of the collapsed Haskouri confederation), and a fraction of the Aït Atta that entered during the Atta confederation's advance towards the Middle Atlas. French Wikipedia adds, citing Couvreur and Lecestre-Rollier, the sedentary Tachelhit-speaking Masmouda tribe of Aït Ouaster, pushed north by Tamazight-speaking nomads expanding from pre-Saharan areas.

“A mosaic of social and linguistic groups bound together by belonging to the territory more than by common descent” — the French source's description of how the valley's population formed, contradicting the romantic picture of a single-lineage tribe.

Immediate neighbours are: Aït Abbas and Aït Bou Oulli to the west and north-west, Aït M'Hamed to the north, Zaouiat Ahansal to the east, and Aït Atta and Imeghrane to the south across the passes. The valley's people long watched the Dadès – Aït Bouguemez – Aït M'Hamed pass towards the plain's centres, giving them strategic importance beyond their numbers.

Chapter Four

Transhumance, farming and water: an economy of duality

The common mistake is to classify the valley's people as either nomadic herders or settled farmers. The historical reality is duality: farming in the irrigated lowland, and herding on the slopes and high mountains.

Transhumance in both directions

Southwards in winter: the harsh winter pushed herders to leave the territory for the southern slopes (Imeghrane and Dadès) at the start of each winter, returning in spring — a relationship organised by old custom, still continuing today but under the supervision of state representatives (the caïdat). We do not know for certain whether everyone left, or whether herders migrated while farmers stayed to guard the fields; most likely tasks were divided within the same group.

Northwards in summer: in the opposite direction, semi-nomadic herders from the southern Atlas and Sagro, led by the Aït Atta, climb to the valley's high pastures from early spring to late summer. The marabouts of Ahansal organised this relationship, and old agreements still allow these nomads access to some of the valley's agdals, including the Agdal of Timda. In autumn, the nomads bartered their animal products (wool, milk, cheese, livestock) for grain and dried fruit from the settled farmers.

The agdal: closing the pasture so it lives Documented

The agdal system is the cornerstone of managing common resources: a temporary closure — decided by the customary council (ajma'a) — of a pasture or forest, with set opening and closing dates, penalties for violators, and guards to monitor. High pastures stay closed until late May so vegetation regenerates before the herds arrive, and village forests follow precise rules on when and how much wood may be cut.

Researchers have studied it as a successful model of managing “the commons” in Elinor Ostrom's terms: a collective right of exclusion, local decision-making, and graduated sanctions. But it has retreated since the drought of the 1980s, due to prolonged drought, pressure on pastures, and families converting to apple farming — today, in many places, it is more a reference rule than a strict system.

Farming on three levels, irrigated by seguias

  • The valley floor, flat, silty and well irrigated: subsistence crops, vegetables, fodder and grain — then, since the end of the Protectorate, commercial crops: potatoes first, then apple orchards.
  • The first unirrigated slopes (bour): dry grain and legumes, often on terraces, where most villages stand.
  • Forests and high pastures: collectively managed, then summer pastures (azaïb: herders' simple summer shelters).

Irrigation is an old network of seguias (channels) fed by karst springs and the river, distributed under a huge number of informal historical agreements between villages — the canals are almost all inter-village. The naïb, appointed by the douar's jma'a, oversees water distribution and monitors the seguias. In recent decades, water committees have become associations registered with the caïdat — the first experiment at Aït Imi in 2003, at the residents' initiative.

Today, farmers say the irrigation turn can reach 20–35 days depending on the weather, the maintenance fee can reach 50 dirhams per hour of irrigation paid to the association, with fines for violators — and solar pumping has become common, a technical shift that changes the balance of old rights based on natural flow. (Médias24, 2025)

Chapter Five

Successive dynasties and zawiyas: history by proxy, not by local event

Honesty is required: there is no dated local account linking Aït Bouguemez to a specific event under the Almoravids, Almohads, Marinids, Saadians or early Alaouites. What follows is the regional framework within which the valley is understood.

Almoravids and Almohads: the Haskouris between siege and support Research hypothesis

Khouya, following Ahmed Toufiq, considers it likely that the Aït Bouguemez and Aït Abbas belonged to the Haskouri confederation, entrenched in the Atlas since the beginnings of Islam. At the start of the Almohad movement, the Haskouris supported the Almohads — support Toufiq attributed to the siege the Almoravids imposed through a chain of castles and fortresses at the contact zones between plain and mountain, to prevent the Haskouris descending to the plain.

The Haskouri territory was fertile and strategic: a water network allowing farming and herding together, passes for north–south movement, and control of trade routes, including the Tizi n'Aït Bou Oulli pass, formerly called “Tizi n'Tkarn”, the merchants' pass. This does not mean the Aït Bouguemez “took part” in a specific battle, but that they were part of a large tribal bloc that politically moved with the Almohads against the Almoravids, then split from them.

From the 12th century: the confederation fragments, the tribe is born

Khouya supposes the decisive phase begins in the 12th century: the Haskouris split from the Almohads, the giant confederation divided, and small groups emerged, more attached to the land with clearer territorial boundaries — and in these conditions, most likely, the territories of Aït Abbas and Aït Bouguemez formed.

Oral account says the Aït Abbas split from the Hantifa alliance over a conflict about farmland and water. Oral account No comparable split story is told in the same detail for Aït Bouguemez, but the logic is the same: fragmentation and final settlement. In the Marinid–Wattasid era new elements entered — some planted by successive dynasties — reshaping the tribal structure, without precise names or dates preserved.

Centuries of turmoil and “the Year of Hunger”

From the Marinid era to the mid-19th century: declining central authority, tribal conflicts, and waves of drought, plague and famine. Echoes of those years can still be heard from elderly people relaying their grandparents, especially drought years known as “Asgas n Laz” — the Year of Hunger, without precise dating, and without knowing whether it means one specific year or a recurring pattern of lean years. Oral memory

In these conditions collective granaries (igherman) regained importance, but with a new function: defence and refuge, not just storage. No mention is made of a specific role for the valley in the Saadian era or early Alaouite period — and the silence here is evidence of political marginality, not of absence of population: the valley existed, farmed and inhabited, but it was not a stage for events recorded in dynastic chronicles.

Zawiyas and saints: local Islam and the mediation of Ahansal Documented in studies by Gellner and Morsy

If the Makhzen was absent, Islam was not. A pattern of “maraboutic Islam” spread in the central Atlas, based on zawiyas and mediating saints: they guarantee peace between tribes, supervise customary elections, arbitrate, and secure roads and markets — without being a state.

The valley's most famous neighbour in this respect is the Zawiya of Ahansal: founded by Sidi Saïd al-Ahansali in the 13th century according to local account, then Sidi Saïd ben Youssef founded in the 17th century the Hansali order and the zawiya in the institutional sense. Ernest Gellner studied it in “Saints of the Atlas”, and Magali Morsy did too, as a “maraboutic state” with no army and no taxes, based on baraka (blessing) and mediation. Its leader Sidi Mha had direct influence over the Aït Bouguemez in the early 20th century, in resistance and negotiation alike.

Inside the valley itself: the Zawiya of Oulmzi, which residents of the whole tribe visit every year, and the shrine of Sidi Moussa at Timit — and these collective visits were themselves a political act reaffirming the tribe's unity above the division of fractions.

Chapter Six

Land of siba: organised tribal independence, not chaos

“Bilad as-siba” is the Moroccan historical term for regions that did not pay taxes regularly to the Makhzen, did not accept its judges and caïds, and managed their affairs through their customs and councils — while generally recognising the Sultan as religious imam and dealing with him through intermediaries.

Rotating chieftaincy… then capture

Until the 19th century the system was based on elected, rotating chieftaincy: each fraction presented an “amghar” (chief) who ruled for a full year, and the overall chieftaincy rotated among the three fractions. His tasks: organising relations between fractions and “bones”, resolving disputes beyond the douar council, and joining the tribe's external delegations (lajma'at / ikhtarn).

But the system began to break down from the mid-19th century: certain families captured the chieftaincy — including the Aït Glaout family in Aït Bouguemez (and Aït Idir in Aït Abbas) — without reaching the level of the great caïdal families such as the Glaoua. This shift later paved the way for the colonial caïdal system to penetrate society, because it found families ready for the role of permanent intermediary.

Councils that manage everything

  • Ajma'a / Lajma'at: a council of 12 members from the tribe's chiefs, most knowledgeable in custom, whose word is sometimes heard even among neighbouring tribes.
  • Ajmu' n Douar: the douar council, attended by a representative of each family, run by the “moqaddem” elected for four months. It has forms: n ljame' (the mosque and imam, and integrating young adults after Ramadan through the rite of measuring the neck with a thread), n laamt (weddings and celebrations, with a president called amghar n laamt who knows the dances and songs), n nnaïb (water affairs).

Treaties: brothers in milk, and a sacrifice that is not refused Customs described; events oral

Tafrkant / Agartchou: a treaty concluded by collecting the milk of women from both disputing sides in one vessel (ahallab) from which all the men of both sides drink, becoming “brothers in milk” — a liquid “that one does not dare disobey”. Echoes of the Agartchou treaty concluded in the days of siba between Aït Skat and the “bones” of Aït Tahartout and Aït Aouli are still in force today, as both sides avoid attacking those covered by the treaty.

The sacrifice / casting of shame: shedding the blood of an animal sacrificed in acknowledgement of fault and request for forgiveness, undertaken by the “Ikhtarn n Tqabilt” (the tribe's level-headed men), whose request is refused only by one who exposes himself to “ammoutl” (calamity) in local belief.

These institutions have their political vocabulary: tamkhmakt (the capacity to receive high delegations with generosity and resources), tiryuza (manhood in the sense of keeping one's word), oudmawn (the “faces” — the senior mediators). Concepts that translate neither into Western “democracy” nor into “feudalism”, but into a system of honour and mediation.

Main source for this chapter and the chapters on customary organisation: Mohamed Khouya, “The Central High Atlas: From Inherited Systems to the Imposed System”, Atlas Scoop.

Chapter Seven

The French Protectorate and resistance (1912–1956)

“Resistance” and “negotiation” were not contradictory positions held by the whole tribe at one moment, but parallel paths among different fractions and notables — which explains the oscillation between confrontation and accommodation.

1912–1915: first contact and the negotiating delegation

The Protectorate treaty was signed on 30 March 1912. The first contact between Aït Bouguemez resisters and the coloniser came in late 1912, during Colonel Mangin's campaign on Demnate and Ntifa, and intensified after the coloniser entered Aït Messaad and Aït Abbas. The valley had strategic importance as a passage for resisters towards submitted tribes and Demnate without using the Azilal road.

In January 1915 the Aït Abbas and Aït Bouguemez sent a joint delegation of notables to Caïd Abdullah Achtou at Ntifa al-Jabal, to discuss entering obedience to the Makhzen — the same year the Bureau of Indigenous Affairs was created at Tanant. Another account adds that a delegation from Aït Bouguemez visited the Zawiya of Tanaghmelt and consulted its moqaddem on resistance or negotiation, and he advised them to enter France's alliance without fighting it, and that a September report stated part of the tribe was ready to contact the French via Ntifa.

1918: El Glaoui's harka and the looting on the return The famous number is an oral account

The two tribes did not escape the brutality of Thami El Glaoui when his harka, directed in 1918 against the Aït Atta led by Sidi Mha, passed through their territories. Gustave Babin, an eyewitness who accompanied Colonel Noguès, spoke of El Glaoui's harka and “the savage horde that caused the looting”, attributing it to the tribe's relative wealth, which made El Glaoui and his armies salivate.

Oral account speaks at length about El Glaoui's return after failing to subdue Sidi Mha's fighters and venting his anger on the two tribes: he is said to have dragged on his return more than 140 calves, all from Aït Bouguemez, and a significant number of sheep and cattle from Aït Abbas. The number is an oral account, not an administrative count, but it reflects the scale of the shock in collective memory — and the deep enmity towards the Glaoua that would appear four years later.

September 1922: Battle of Oued Aït Hakim Documented — Peyron 2021 and press

The most famous military event in the valley's modern history. The people of Aït Bouguemez were self-governing, though under the influence of Sidi Mha of Ahansal, when the forces of Caïd Thami El Glaoui, ally of the French, attacked them:

  • Several thousand horsemen of El Glaoui's harka attacked about 2,000 fighters from Aït Bouguemez and Aït Atta in Oued Aït Hakim, one of the valley's branches.
  • The attack was repelled, El Glaoui's horsemen were defeated and forced to withdraw towards Marrakech.

The battle should not be inflated into a “battle of independence”: it was a local clash in the context of the French “pacification” of the Atlas, in which the Aït Atta took part as seasonal allies and neighbours, ending with El Glaoui's withdrawal, not the fall of the Protectorate. But it remained in local memory as a sign that the valley is not easily invaded, and that “El Glaoui” — symbol of the caïd collaborating with colonisation — can be defeated.

Source: Michael Peyron, “Berbers of Morocco: A History of Resistance” (2021, p. 128), via French Wikipedia; and Moroccan newspaper Libération.

1923 and after: rallying and relative calm

In June 1923 Sidi Mha rallied to the French authorities and the Makhzen, and calm returned to the region. After the submission of Aït M'Hamed and the creation of a command post there, Aït Abbas and Aït Bouguemez became attached to the Aït M'Hamed command post, and local leaderships emerged, including the Aït Glaout family that had captured the chieftaincy.

France generally worked to undermine the tribal system and empty it into institutions under surveillance: Bureaus of Indigenous Affairs and customary courts, so the French officer became the “anflous” (the sage), and the bureau became the councils of elders in another form.

Do not confuse: the famous Battle of Bou Gafer (13 February – 25 March 1933), led by Assou Oubasslam in Jbel Sagro, is a battle of the Aït Atta, not of Aït Bouguemez — though it concerns the valley as a neighbour and seasonal ally of the Aït Atta, and as the conclusion of the French “pacification” of all Morocco. Confusing the two is common in popular writing.
Chapter Eight

After independence (1956–today): from isolation to market and tourism

A new state, and the old structure does not die

After Morocco's independence in 1956 the tribal structure was recast into administrative divisions: provinces, caïdats, rural communes, sheikhs and moqaddems. Khouya considers that the state tried to erase the tribal system from collective memory and succeeded only partly: its structures cracked but its “hard cores” still work — and this analysis is the researcher's opinion, not a neutral fact: elections are guided by inherited culture, the party becomes a “new zawiya”, and the civic association a form of the old ajma'a — which explains the success of water associations and women's cooperatives in the valley where top-down projects failed.

1970s–1980s: tourism arrives before the road

In the early 1970s foreign tourists began to arrive — some, according to a local account, originally came to fish for trout in the “green valley”, then were taken by the mountains and organised trips from Europe. In the early 1980s mountain tourism developed after the founding of the Mountain Professions Training Centre at Tabant in 1984 — the only one of its kind in Morocco and the Arab world at the time — graduating about 40 qualified staff a year according to local press, making the valley the unofficial “capital” of Moroccan mountain guiding.

In parallel began the agricultural transformation: from the 1980s the valley chose market-oriented farming after centuries of subsistence farming — potatoes first after the end of the Protectorate, then apples, almost a monoculture in the valley floor especially since about 2005, until Aït Bouguemez became, according to the Tadla Regional Office for Agricultural Development, the largest apple production base in the Béni Mellal – Khénifra region.

2002: the paved road, the turning point

The biggest event in the valley's contemporary history, by consensus of local press: connecting the valley to the paved road in 2002 (some tourist sources say 2001 — a one-year difference likely reflecting the gap between completion of works and official opening).

Within a few years visitors multiplied many times over, and the number of tourist lodges rose from four to about 80. Aït Bouguemez came to be two hours from Azilal, three and a half hours from Béni Mellal, and four and a half hours from Marrakech. The Sunday market at Tabant became a weekly commercial and social centre, and associations and cooperatives multiplied.

But the road did not solve everything: snow still closes the valley for periods in winter, the mountain road is fragile in the face of floods and landslides — and water, not the road, became the first challenge in recent drought years.

Population of Tabant commune: growth despite emigration

Figures from the High Commission for Planning (via CityPopulation). The growth reflects relative improvement in health and education and many families staying thanks to apples and tourism — but it hides internal disparity: high douars gradually emptying, others near the road and market growing.

Today: apples, drought and protest over water

Apples have become the first source of livelihood for many families, but also a source of fragility: expanding orchards threaten the diversity of fruit trees (walnut, almond and others), increase pressure on water, and expose farmers to price volatility — 12 dirhams per kilogram at the Casablanca wholesale market in the 2026 season according to Médias24, a price that does not always reflect production and transport costs.

In July 2025 the residents of Aït Bouguemez protested, demanding healthcare, an end to isolation through road repairs, internet connection and water provision, after lean years — an event carried by national press, reflecting that “the Happy Valley” is not immune to the national water crisis.

In October 2026 a call for tenders was announced to equip the Mountain Professions Training Centre at Aït Bouguemez (Tabant commune) at an estimated cost of 3,144,966 dirhams, under the Regional Project Implementation Agency of the Béni Mellal – Khénifra region, to train young people in mountain professions, nature sports and ecotourism — a project symbolically linking the legacy of the 1984 centre to today's sustainable tourism, but still at the equipment stage, not graduation.

Sources: Hespress (protest, 14 July 2025); Rue20 (2026 centre, 27 Oct 2026); Médias24 (prices and farming).

Chapter Nine

Social organisation and architecture: the family as nucleus, the granary as heart

Nested units, not a single pyramid

  • The family (takat): the nucleus of daily organisation — a unit of production and consumption, though individuals have recently tended towards independence from the extended family.
  • The “bone” (ighs): the large patrilineal family; land division was done at its level, and its importance has declined today — but it suddenly regains strength in elections if two candidates come from two different “bones”.
  • The fraction: three in Aït Bouguemez; its importance was political in the past, and today it appears only on occasions, especially elections.
  • Location and douar: the douar is the most lively unit today, with its council, moqaddem and naïb.
  • The tribe: the highest unit; it preserves the name, borders and some values, but its old institutions (overall chief and ajma'a) have disappeared, replaced by modern institutions drawing on the heritage: the rural commune council and the civic association.

The tribe therefore did not die, but transformed: from an armed political organisation into a territorial and cultural identity, from a customary council into an association, from a rotating chief into an elected commune president — with the logic of “bone” and fraction still working beneath the surface.

Women's role is central even if less visible in political sources: women weave carpets in cooperatives, carry harvests, manage home and water in the absence of men who are herding or migrated, take part in fertility rites at Sidi Moussa — and it is in “women's milk” that treaties are concluded, meaning women's bodies and milk were symbolically the guarantee of peace between tribes. A role that deserves a dedicated study not yet done for the valley itself.

Building with tabout and the tighremt

Houses are traditionally built with tabout (earth rammed in wooden moulds without cement or sand), with stone where available, fragrant juniper wood for roofs and pillars, and plaster for finishing.

The traditional house until the first third of the 20th century followed the tighremt pattern: a fortified square house of one or two storeys, with corner towers, few small openings, an inner courtyard and a clear defensive function. Then a less enclosed pattern spread: rooms around a courtyard, wider windows and a balcony on the façade. Today cement and brick are advancing across the valley, especially in Tabant and along the road, threatening the craft of tabout builders — though it remains alive in restorations and tourism projects.

Ighrem of Sidi Moussa: the only circular granary Description documented Dating to 17th c. is an account

Almost every village had an ighrem — a fortified collective granary for storing grain and precious belongings, under collective guard, which in times of turmoil also became a defensive refuge. The most famous is the Ighrem of Sidi Moussa near the douar of Timit, on a conical hill rising about 200 m above the valley centre at the meeting of the two streams:

  • It is the only circular collective granary in the High Atlas built with tabout, with a doubled circular wall reinforced by four towers according to the Ministry of Culture file.
  • Two storeys: Sidi Moussa's tomb on the ground floor, and 30 cells (each cell for a family) served by a circular gallery on the upper floor, with massive juniper pillars carrying the roofs.
  • Sidi Moussa is attributed in local account to the 17th century: he settled on a rock overlooking the valley, then his tomb was incorporated after his death into the douar's granary. Today it is also a shrine: women especially visit it seeking fertility and healing, and scenes from the Moroccan series “Roummana wa Bartal” were filmed there, so some of its caves are known as “the caves of Roummana and Bartal”.

Other igherman include: Ighrem of Sidi Chita (Sidi Shams) above the douar of Idoukalen — the second of the two granaries outside douars associated with a saint's tomb — and igherman at Ibakallioune and elsewhere, many today ruins or tourist sites and small museums. There is no “kasbah” in the valley in the grand Marrakech sense (such as Aït Ben Haddou), but a network of square family house-fortresses (tighermat) with corner towers, some of circular geometry at Aït Imi.

An important common correction: some tourist press says “the Kasbah of Sidi Moussa is more than 430 years old and classified as UNESCO World Heritage”. The figure of 430 years roughly matches the 17th century, but the “World Heritage” classification is inaccurate: the valley is part of the UNESCO M'Goun Global Geopark (joining the network in 2014, UNESCO global designation in 2015) — which is not inscription on the World Heritage List. Moroccan collective granaries in general were the subject of a nomination project prepared by the Ministry of Culture, not a settled inscription.
Chapter Ten

Cultural heritage: what is seen, heard and woven

Tangible heritage

  • Rock engravings at Tizi n'Tirghist and the neighbourhood, and dinosaur tracks at Ibakallioune.
  • Traditional water mills near Aït Imi (seven mills according to some tourist sources) working by water power to grind grain, part of the old irrigation system.
  • Old mosques and zawiyas, including the Zawiya of Oulmzi, and douar mosques whose affairs are managed by Ajmu' n Ljame'.
  • Two environmental recognitions: the valley is part of the UNESCO M'Goun Global Geopark (the first geopark in Morocco, Africa and the Arab world), and of the Ramsar site “Upper Lakhdar Valley”, a wetland of international importance — recognitions that do not protect cultural heritage in themselves, but place the valley on the map of nature conservation and sustainable development.

Intangible heritage

  • Dance and music: Ahwash and Ahidous with collective songs and circular dances enlivening weddings, festivals and harvests — some of which preserve the memory of old battles, as Khouya notes. The Ahwash of Aït Bouguemez and Aït Abbas is similar, as is “playing with gunpowder” at weddings.
  • Weaving: Women's cooperative carpets (including the Tikniouine cooperative) are woven from local wool on vertical looms, with natural dyes (walnut for brown, flower petals for yellow, a red root for red) and geometric motifs that differ from village to village — with colours said to be softer than the bright carpets of Azilal. A large carpet takes more than a month, and women work in two teams.
  • Tattooing on the chin and forehead of elderly women: a mark of identity and beauty on its way to disappearing, though its motifs recur in carpets.
  • Rites and knowledge: the annual Boughanim tour after ploughing, visiting Sidi Moussa and the Zawiya of Oulmzi, the agdal calendar, water distribution, tabout building, beekeeping and herbal medicine — oral knowledge threatened with loss as young people emigrate.
Chapter Eleven

Timeline: from 185 million years ago to October 2026

Filter events by their level of documentation — not all milestones in this history have the same degree of certainty.

About 183–185 million years ago

Dinosaur tracks at Ibakallioune

Geologically documented

Footprints of sauropods and theropods on Lower Jurassic limestone slabs — geological time, not human.

Lower Pleistocene

The ancient lake and the valley floor

Geomorphologically documented

A natural dam at Tizi n'Tighza formed a lake covering the valley, whose silt made today's fertile plain.

About 2500–1200 BCE (estimate)

Rock engravings at Tizi n'Tirghist

Hypothesis

Two readings: a battle commemorated over pastures, or herders fleeing Sahara drought. Press estimate for some engravings: about 4,500 years — without laboratory dating.

Before the Almohads – 12th c.

The Haskouri confederation: formation, support, fragmentation

Research hypothesis

In Toufiq's and Khouya's reading: the confederation supports the Almohads against the Almoravid siege, then splits from them and fragments — giving birth to small tribal territories including Aït Bouguemez.

12th c. — early Almohad era

Al-Baydhaq's mention

Textually documented

First known written reference: Aït Bouguemez among the Sanhaja of the Shade (Bani Sattat) in “Al-Ansab fi Ma'rifat al-Ashab”. The name then disappears from texts for centuries.

13th c.

Founding of the Zawiya of Ahansal

Local account + studies

Sidi Saïd al-Ahansali founds the zawiya that will become the reference for mediation across the central Atlas, with direct influence on the valley.

13th–15th c.

Encirclement and retreat

Research interpretation

Banu Hilal from the north and Banu Ma'qil from the Drâa side cut trade and news routes for the Haskoura of the Shade, and Demnate hides what lies behind it.

17th c. (according to account)

Sidi Moussa and the Hansali order

Account — approximate date

Sidi Moussa settles above the valley and his circular ighrem is built around his tomb; Sidi Saïd ben Youssef founds the Hansali order in the institutional sense.

Until mid-19th c.

The era of organised siba

Partly documented + oral

Rotating chieftaincy, an ajma'a of 12 chiefs, agdal managing pastures, defensive igherman — and the years of “the Year of Hunger” (Asgas n Laz) in memory, without a specific year.

Mid-19th c.

Aït Glaout capture the chieftaincy

Khouya's research

End of local rotation: the Aït Glaout family captures the tribe's political affairs in Aït Bouguemez, and Aït Idir in Aït Abbas.

1912

Protectorate treaty and first contact

Research summary

The Protectorate is signed on 30 March; first contact late in the year during Mangin's campaign on Demnate and Ntifa.

January 1915

Joint negotiating delegation

Documented in Khouya

Delegation of Aït Bouguemez and Aït Abbas to Caïd Abdullah Achtou at Ntifa to discuss obedience; creation of the Bureau of Indigenous Affairs at Tanant the same year.

1918

El Glaoui's harka passes and the looting on return

Babin's testimony + account

El Glaoui's harka against Sidi Mha passes through both tribes' territory; oral account: more than 140 calves dragged from Aït Bouguemez on the return.

September 1922

Battle of Oued Aït Hakim

Documented

About 2,000 fighters from Aït Bouguemez and Aït Atta repel several thousand of El Glaoui's horsemen, who withdraw towards Marrakech.

June 1923

Sidi Mha rallies and relative calm

Documented

Sidi Mha rallies to the French and the Makhzen; both tribes become attached to the Aït M'Hamed command post.

1933

Bou Gafer — in the neighbourhood, not the valley

Documented — context only

Battle of the Aït Atta led by Assou Oubasslam in Sagro (13 February – 25 March), the conclusion of the French “pacification”. It is not an Aït Bouguemez battle.

1956

Moroccan independence

General framework

Gradual integration of the valley into modern administration: caïdats and rural communes, with customary structures still working beneath the surface.

1970s–1984

Tourism arrives, and the Mountain Professions Centre

Press and university research

Foreign tourists from the early 1970s; founding of the Mountain Professions Training Centre at Tabant in 1984, the only one of its kind in Morocco and the Arab world at the time.

1980s – about 2005

From subsistence to market

Studies and Médias24

Market farming: potatoes then apples in near-monoculture on the valley floor; retreat of the agdal with the long 1980s drought.

2002 (or 2001)

The paved road

Local press

The great turning point: tourist lodges from 4 to about 80, and the valley two hours from Azilal.

2003

First water committee as an association

Romagny 2008

Residents of Aït Imi turn the customary water committee into a registered association — the direct heir of old water customs.

2014 / 2015

M'Goun Global Geopark

UNESCO

Joining the Geoparks network in 2014, then UNESCO global designation in 2015 — it is not inscription on the World Heritage List.

July 2025

Protest over water, health and roads

National press

Valley residents protest demanding water, health services, road repairs and internet, after lean years.

October 2026

Re-equipping the Mountain Professions Centre

Regional press

Call for tenders at an estimated cost of 3,144,966 dirhams to equip the Mountain Professions Training Centre at Tabant — still at the equipment stage.

Chapter Twelve

What is documented, what is account, and where are the gaps?

An honest answer to the question “the history of Aït Bouguemez” requires also saying what we do not know.

Well documented

  • Geography and geology: dinosaurs, the ancient lake, altitudes.
  • Al-Baydhaq's single mention, and the general Haskouri framework in Toufiq.
  • The events of 1915, 1918, 1922 and 1923 in their general framework, even if detailed numbers differ.
  • The customary structure: chieftaincy, ajma'a, naïb, agdal.
  • Contemporary transformations: the 2002 road, apples, population, geopark.

Hypotheses needing verification

  • Precise Haskouri affiliation and the date of the confederation's fragmentation.
  • The origin of the Aït Ouaster, and the entry of the Iklawan and Aït Atta.
  • Dating and interpreting the rock engravings, and attributing caves to “the Portuguese”.
  • Dating Sidi Moussa and Sidi Chita to the 17th century — from account and style, not from a founding document or published radiocarbon.
  • The origin of the name “people of the middle” — linguistically convincing, but not a document.

Accounts preserved, not asserted

  • The split of Aït Abbas from Hantifa, and the Agartchou treaty.
  • The 140 calves looted by El Glaoui in 1918.
  • “The Year of Hunger” (Asgas n Laz) without a specific year.
  • Sidi Moussa's miracles of healing and fertility, and the Boughanim tour.
  • The story of the “Happy Valley” nickname from foreign visitors — never attributed to a primary source.

Six frank gaps the sources did not answer

1 — No local written history for the medieval and early modern periods

No chiefs' names or year-by-year events for the valley before the 19th century in the available sources; everything concerning those centuries is regional reading and hypotheses, not an event-history of the valley itself.

2 — No published archaeological study of settlement of the valley floor

No excavations, radiocarbon dating or systematic cave survey published for the valley floor itself so far.

3 — No detailed account of the Saadian and early Alaouite eras

Nor of specific famines and epidemics with dates — even though the valley was inhabited and farmed throughout those centuries.

4 — No historical statistics before the Protectorate

No population or production figures and no Makhzen tax records specific to the valley before the 20th century.

5 — Women's role has not been given a dedicated study

Beyond general tourist mentions, there is no dedicated study of women and women's cooperatives in the valley itself.

6 — Circulated numbers not settled

Number of douars (27 or 30 or 32?), number of lodges (80?), number of Sidi Moussa cells (30?) — they differ by counting year and definition, and no single statistical source settles them.

What the next researcher should do: return to the French Indigenous Affairs archives (Tanant, Azilal) and zawiya documents (Ahansal and Tanaghmelt), carry out a field survey of engravings and igherman with scientific dating, and methodically collect oral accounts from elderly people before they are lost — for oral memory here, in the absence of documents, is the indispensable first source, provided it is criticised and cross-checked.
Sources

Sources for this page

This page was built from a documented research report whose sources were read via the web index on 30 October 2026, with no field verification. It contained no local primary document (manuscript, customary deed or zawiya register) specific to Aït Bouguemez, because the sources available on the web do not publish them. The full reference list — Khouya (Atlas Scoop, 2017), Wikipedia “Vallée des Aït Bouguemez”, Romagny et al. (2008), the Ministry of Culture file on collective granaries, Gellner, Médias24, Hespress, CityPopulation/HCP and UNESCO — is detailed in the Arabic version, Sources section.
